question.text: About 40 members of the Parliament in the UK represent this country, home to the cities of Gwynedd and Swansea.
question.clue: This polity's parliament, the Senedd, was created by referendum in 1997, and has had to navigate challenges with the collapse of the coal and steel industries.

swap.leadin: This vessel from the Cunard Line was named after the Roman province that included modern-day Portugal.
swap.text: Name this British ocean liner, the world's largest passenger ship at the time, that was sunk in 1915 off the coast of Ireland.
swap.clue: Travelers on this ship were warned that a "state of war exists" by a newspaper ad plaed by the Imperial German Embassy.

question.leadin: The Mamluks forced this ruler to retire from Crusading by having him stabbed with an allegedly poisoned dagger.
question.text: Name this English king, nicknamed "Longshanks," who won the Battle of Falkirk.
question.clue: This king married his son to Isabella of France, which led this man's grandson to claim the French throne and spark the Hundred Years War.

swap.text: Elizabeth II was proclaimed Queen after the death of this King, her father, who remained in Buckingham Palace during German bombings in World War II.
swap.clue: This king ruled the United Kingdom through World War II until his death in 1952. This man ascended the throne when Prince Edward abdicated the throne to marry the American Wallis Simpson.

question.text: Critiquing the geographic breadth of older studies, Pomeranz preferred a comparison between China's highly-commercialized Yangtze Delta and this country where the Industrial Revolution first took place.
question.answerHtml: Great Britain [or England or the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland or UK or Kingdom of Great Britain]
question.clue: Emperor Hadrian constructed a 73-mile long defensive wall spanning this island.

swap.leadin: Edward II was defeated in this crucial battle of the First War of Scottish Independence.
swap.text: Edward was defeated at this battle while trying to relieve an English force occupying Stirling Castle:
swap.clue: Action in this battle was preceded by an agreement between one commander's brother and Sir Philip Mowbray in which Mowbray's castle garrison would be forced to surrender by June 24.

question.leadin: She isn't Elizabeth I, but this woman made a rousing speech about English courage in anticipation of the Earl of Surrey's victory at Flodden Field.
question.text: The book The Education of A Christian Woman by Juan Luis Vives was commissioned by this wife of Arthur, the son of Henry VII.
question.clue: She served as regent for one year while her husband joined Maximilian I in defeating French forces at Guinegate.

swap.leadin: Like many other revolts, this one began with an attempt to collect taxes.
swap.text: Give this generically named uprising in the 14th century led by Wat Tyler and John Ball. It would be cited 600 years later when the Thatcher government tried to institute what was seen as a poll tax.
swap.clue: One side in this conflict was responsible for the beheading of Robert Hales and Simon of Sudbury, and that side received support from the priest John Ball.

question.leadin: Identify these British prime ministers from the age of Victoria.
question.text: This man served as prime minister four times between 1868 and 1894. Noted for his support of Irish Home Rule, this member of the Liberal Party was a rival of Benjamin Disrael.
question.clue: He lost the support of the Liberal Unionists to Lord Salisbury, and he was publicly blamed for the death of General Gordon.

swap.leadin: Golf has traditionally been traced back to 15th century Scotland.
swap.text: This monarch was seen playing golf at Seton Palace shortly after the death of Lord Darnley. This monarch wrote the Casket Letters to the Earl of Bothwell.
swap.answerHtml: Mary, Queen of Scots [or Mary I of Scotland or Mary Stuart; prompt on Mary or Mary I; reject “Mary Tudor” or “Bloody Mary”]
swap.clue: This monarch abdicated after the Encounter of Carberry Hill.

question.leadin: The book Guilty Men castigated members of the British government who advocated this policy.
question.text: Name this policy of the government of Neville Chamberlain that claimed to have achieved "peace for our time" by making concessions to Adolf Hitler such as in the Munich Agreement.
question.answerHtml: appeasement [or appeasing Nazi Germany or appeasing Adolf Hitler; prompt on answers mentioning avoiding war with Nazi Germany]
question.clue: Edvard Benes was not invited to a meeting orchestrated as part of this policy which was attended by Edouard Daladier.

swap.text: This Roman goddess of the hunt was equivalent to the Greek Artemis.
swap.clue: A fascist Mitford sister shares this forename with a woman who visited Angola as part of her work with the HALO Trust.

question.text: The leader of the British troops at Fashoda was this general, who had just finished wiping the floor with the Mahdists at Omdurman. He would later be killed by a German mime.

swap.leadin: This Dissenter promoted religious toleration with his Remarks on Blackstone's Commentaries.
swap.text: Name this English scientist who discovered what he called "dephlogisticated air", but refused to accept the chemical revolution and reject phlogiston theory.
swap.clue: A meeting with Benjamin Franklin led to the discovery that graphite conducts electricity, which he documented in his book The History of Electricity.

question.leadin: This person's life is attested to in part by four separate wills made from 1394 to 1416, and The Book of Margery Kempe describes a visit regarding their revelations.
question.text: Name this fourteenth-century anchoress and author of the Showings.
question.answerHtml: Julian of Norwich [or Juliana of Norwich; accept Lady Juliana, Dame Juliana or Mother Juliana; prompt on Julian or Juliana alone]

swap.leadin: Answer some questions on succession crises in Scottish history.
swap.text: Scotland's wars of independence began when Alexander III rode his horse off a cliff, and this granddaughter of his and possible betrothed of Edward II died aged 7 at Orkney of sea-sickness, prompting Edward I's invasion.
swap.answerHtml: Margaret, The Maid of Norway [accept either underlined portion]

question.leadin: Despite the repeal of the Combination Acts making trade unions legal, these people were prosecuted based on a 1797 law against swearing oaths.
question.text: Name this group of six farmhands who were sentenced to transportation to Australia in 1834.
question.clue: This group of six "martyrs" that included George Loveless, a cofounder of the Friendly Society of Agricultural Laborers.

swap.text: Among the founding members of the company was Sebastian, an explorer with this surname. Sebastian's father, who also held this surname, led a British expedition to the coast of North America in 1497.
swap.clue: That explorer believed he had reached Asia after discovering Cape North, St. Paul Island, and Miquelon in his ship the Matthew.

question.leadin: The slang and code of miners of this ethnicity in towns like Real del Monte is thought to be a major influence on albur, a form of Mexican wordplay featuring double entendres.
question.text: Name this ethnicity of the miners who founded Mexico's oldest football club in Pachuca. Emigrants of this ethnicity were often nicknamed "cousin Jacks" when working in areas like South Australia's Copper Coast and Michigan's Upper Peninsula.

swap.text: Located near Salisbury, this notorious rotten borough was once the site of a Norman castle and cathedral on a hilltop. By the time of the Reform Act, it was depopulated and sinking into the ground, it still sent two delegates to the House of Commons.
swap.clue: One "rotten borough" that was abolished was this constituency, centered on a hill in Wiltshire. Due to its extremely low population, this constituency was essentially controlled by the Pitt family.
